name: Nature versus Nurture
what: This subtopic examines the historical debate over whether hereditary factors (nature) or environmental factors (nurture) are the primary driver of psychological development. It concludes with the contemporary understanding that the two interact continuously and are rarely separable.
why: The nature-nurture debate is foundational to all of psychology. Understanding that development results from the interaction of both factors, rather than one alone, allows students to critically evaluate claims about why people turn out the way they do.

items.title: I can define hereditary factors and environmental factors and give an example of each
items.what: Hereditary factors are genetically passed from biological parents to offspring and influence development from conception. Environmental factors arise from an individual's physical and social surroundings, including education, culture, peer groups, and early childhood experiences.
items.why: Being able to distinguish between these two types of factors is necessary for analysing case studies and applying the nature-nurture framework to real scenarios.
items.example: A child inheriting a genetic predisposition for depression is a hereditary factor; the child growing up in a household where a parent is frequently absent is an environmental factor.

items.title: I can describe the nature school of thought and its key claim about development
items.what: The nature school of thought holds that development is primarily determined by genetic composition and is largely predestined at birth, meaning traits such as intelligence and personality are inherited regardless of environmental experience.
items.why: Understanding this historical position allows students to identify its strengths, such as the observable heritability of physical traits, and its limitations, such as its inability to explain why identical twins can differ.
items.example: John Locke's 'tabula rasa' is the opposing view; a nature theorist would instead argue that a child born to two mathematically gifted parents is likely to show mathematical aptitude because of inherited traits, not teaching.

items.title: I can describe the nurture school of thought and explain the concept of tabula rasa
items.what: The nurture school of thought holds that humans are born as a blank slate (tabula rasa) and are shaped entirely by their experiences, environment, and social surroundings. John Watson's behaviourism is a key example of this view.
items.why: Understanding the nurture position helps students recognise the significant role of environment and experience in shaping development, particularly through education, parenting, and socioeconomic status.
items.example: A child raised in a bilingual household who becomes fluent in two languages demonstrates the nurture position: the language environment, not genetic predisposition, produced that outcome.

items.title: I can explain genetic predisposition and what it does and does not guarantee
items.what: Genetic predisposition is the increased likelihood of developing certain traits or conditions if certain environmental conditions are met. It raises the probability of an outcome but does not guarantee it.
items.why: Genetic predisposition is a nuanced concept that sits between pure nature and pure nurture; understanding it prevents students from overstating genetic determinism.
items.example: A person whose parent has clinical depression has a higher probability of developing depression than the general population, but may never develop it if their environment does not provide the triggering conditions.

items.title: I can explain the contemporary understanding that nature and nurture interact to influence development
items.what: Contemporary psychology holds that hereditary and environmental factors are roughly equivalent in influence and operate in a continual, reciprocal relationship rather than independently. Genes can shape how individuals respond to environments, and environments can determine whether genetic predispositions are expressed.
items.why: This interactionist position is the current scientific consensus and is essential for answering exam questions that involve applying nature and nurture to case studies.
items.example: A child born with a warm, sociable temperament (hereditary) may be drawn to more social environments, which in turn further develops their social and emotional skills, demonstrating the reciprocal loop between nature and nurture.
